abstract: Listeners can experience difficulties with spatial hearing and speech understanding in complex acoustic environments despite near-normal hearing thresholds. Cochlear synaptopathy, which reduces auditory nerve input without elevating thresholds, is one candidate mechanism, but how this peripheral deafferentation disrupts binaural processing remains unclear. We adapted a physiologically constrained computational model incorporating the auditory periphery, spherical and globular bushy cells of the cochlear nucleus and the lateral superior olive (LSO) to examine the separate and combined effects of reduced afferent input and degraded spike timing. Synaptopathy was modeled as loss of auditory nerve inputs to bushy cells, whereas central myelin dysfunction was modeled as increased temporal jitter in bushy cell outputs. Loss of auditory nerve input substantially reduced bushy cell firing rates without degrading phase locking. Despite this preserved temporal precision, binaural tuning in the LSO declined disproportionately, where moderate afferent loss produced substantial reductions in sensitivity to interaural envelope phase differences. In contrast, temporal jitter preserved bushy cell firing rates but degraded phase locking and binaural tuning. Selective loss of input to excitatory versus inhibitory pathways produced opposite changes in overall LSO firing rate, yet both reduced binaural interaction. These results identify two mechanistically distinct routes to impaired binaural coding: too few precisely timed spikes, and a sufficient number of spikes arriving with inadequate temporal precision. These results predict that correcting myelin-related timing deficits alone would leave substantial binaural coding impairment when cochlear deafferentation persists, motivating interventions that address both diminished afferent drive and impaired transmission.
